html:
Lingít Aaní is the homeland of the Tlingit, a people of the coast and islands of what is now Southeast Alaska, from Yakutat Bay south to the Portland Canal, with inland groups in Yukon and British Columbia.

The Tlingit lived from salmon, halibut and sea mammals in rich coastal waters. Society was divided into two halves, Raven and Eagle (or Wolf), and into clans that owned crests, songs and lands, shown on totem poles and in Chilkat woven blankets. Wealth was given away at the potlatch. Their language is distantly related to the Athabaskan languages and to Eyak. The Haida are their southern neighbours.

From the 1790s Russian America pushed into their land to hunt sea otters. The Tlingit destroyed the first Russian fort at Sitka in 1802, and the Russians retook the site in 1804. After the Alaska Purchase of 1867 they came under the United States. The Tlingit activist Elizabeth Peratrovich helped win Alaska's anti-discrimination law of 1945. See also Tlingit and the inland Teslin Tlingit.
